title: What are Git's four locations for code (working directory, staging area, local repository, remote repository), and which commands move changes between them (`add`, `commit`, `push`, `fetch`/`pull`)?
shortTitle: Git's four locations for code and the commands that move changes between them

s1_definition.profdef: Git organizes your code across four conceptual locations. The working directory is the set of files you actually edit on disk. The staging area, also called the index, is where you assemble exactly which changes go into the next commit. The local repository is the dot-git database on your machine that stores committed snapshots. The remote repository is the shared copy on a server such as GitHub. You move changes forward with git add (working directory to staging) and git commit (staging to local repository), and share them with git push (local to remote); you bring others' work down with git fetch and git pull (remote to local).
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine processing transactions at National Bank of India. The working directory is your desk where you scribble and edit draft forms. The staging area is the tray where you place only the specific forms you have decided to submit in this batch. The local repository is your personal locked drawer where submitted batches are permanently filed as dated snapshots. The remote repository is the central bank vault that every branch shares. git add moves a form from your desk into the submission tray, git commit files the tray's contents into your drawer as one dated batch, git push sends your filed batches to the central vault, and git fetch or pull brings the vault's latest batches back to you.
s1_definition.oneliner: Working directory, staging area, local repo, remote repo — add stages, commit saves locally, push shares upward, and fetch or pull brings changes down.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Git organizes your code across four conceptual locations. The working directory is the set of files you actually edit on disk. The staging area, also called the index, is where you assemble exactly which changes go into the next commit. The local repository is the dot-git database on your machine that stores committed snapshots. The remote repository is the shared copy on a server such as GitHub. You move changes forward with git add (working directory to staging) and git commit (staging to local repository), and share them with git push (local to remote); you bring others' work down with git fetch and git pull (remote to local).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine processing transactions at National Bank of India. The working directory is your desk where you scribble and edit draft forms. The staging area is the tray where you place only the specific forms you have decided to submit in this batch. The local repository is your personal locked drawer where submitted batches are permanently filed as dated snapshots. The remote repository is the central bank vault that every branch shares. git add moves a form from your desk into the submission tray, git commit files the tray's contents into your drawer as one dated batch, git push sends your filed batches to the central vault, and git fetch or pull brings the vault's latest batches back to you.

**One line to remember:** Working directory, staging area, local repo, remote repo — add stages, commit saves locally, push shares upward, and fetch or pull brings changes down.

sections.s2_technical:
The working directory is simply the folder of files you see and edit. When you change a file, that change exists only here and is called unstaged or modified. Git knows the file differs from the last committed version, but it has not been told that you intend to include this change in the next snapshot. Running git status lists these modified files in red as "changes not staged for commit."

The staging area, also called the index, is Git's distinctive middle step and often the part newcomers find strange. It is a holding area where you declare exactly which changes belong in the next commit. You might have edited five files but only want to commit three of them as one logical change; the staging area lets you include just those three. You move a change from the working directory into staging with git add, naming specific files like git add src/Transfer.java or everything with git add dot. Staged changes appear in green in git status as "changes to be committed." This two-step design lets you craft clean, focused commits instead of dumping every unrelated edit together.

The local repository is the dot-git directory inside your project. When you run git commit, Git takes everything currently in the staging area and records it as a new permanent snapshot, a commit, with a unique hash, your author information, a timestamp, and a message. This commit lives entirely on your machine — no network is involved, which is why Git is called a distributed version control system and why you can commit on a plane with no internet. The local repository holds your entire branch history locally.

The remote repository is a shared copy hosted on a server like GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket, which the whole team uses as the common meeting point. Your commits are not visible to anyone else until you publish them. git push uploads the commits from your local repository branch to the matching branch on the remote, making them available to teammates. Push only works cleanly if your local branch is ahead of the remote and not behind; if the remote has commits you lack, Git rejects the push and asks you to integrate first.

Bringing others' work down has two commands with an important distinction. git fetch downloads new commits from the remote into your local repository but does NOT change your working directory or your current branch — it updates the remote-tracking references like origin/main so you can inspect what changed before integrating. git pull is a convenience that does a fetch followed immediately by a merge (or a rebase if configured) into your current branch, so it both downloads and applies the changes in one step. A senior-level nuance I always mention: fetch is the safer, more deliberate choice because it lets you review incoming changes before merging, whereas pull can surprise you with an immediate merge commit or conflict. There are also two commands worth naming for completeness that move changes backward: git restore unstages or discards working-directory changes, and git reset moves the branch pointer and can unstage commits. The mental model to carry is a one-way forward pipeline — edit in the working directory, stage with add, save locally with commit, share with push — and a downward flow with fetch and pull to receive others' work.
sections.s3_banking:
A National Bank of India engineer is adding a transfer-limit feature and must move the change cleanly through all four Git locations while also incorporating a teammate's recent work.

Problem 1 — the engineer edited three files but only two belong to this logical change; the third is an unrelated experiment. This is exactly what the staging area solves — git add only the two relevant files so the commit is focused and reviewable.

Problem 2 — the commit must be saved even though the engineer is on a train with no internet. This is exactly why the local repository exists — git commit records the snapshot locally with no network needed.

Problem 3 — a teammate pushed changes to the same file while the engineer worked. This is exactly why fetch and pull exist — fetch to inspect the incoming changes safely first, then integrate before pushing.

The mini-project is a git command walkthrough that edits a TransferLimitService, stages selectively, commits locally, fetches and integrates a teammate's change, and finally pushes. The Java class is the real code flowing through the four locations.

```
transfers-service/
└── src/
    ├── main/java/com/bank/transfers/
    │   ├── TransferLimitService.java
    │   └── Experiment.java            (unrelated edit, NOT committed)
    └── test/java/com/bank/transfers/
```

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Confirm which files live in which location at any moment.
git status                 # working dir (red) vs staging (green)
git diff                   # unstaged changes (working dir vs staging)
git diff --staged          # staged changes (staging vs last commit)
git log --oneline -5       # local repository history
git log --oneline origin/main -5   # remote-tracking view (after fetch)

# Run the tests before pushing.
mvn test
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: the engineer edits TransferLimitService.java, its test, and an unrelated Experiment.java, and must move only the first two to the remote while incorporating a teammate's change.

Step 1: All three edits exist in the working directory. git status shows them in red as modified. Nothing is tracked for the next commit yet; the changes exist only on disk.

Step 2: The engineer runs git add on the two relevant files. They move into the staging area and now appear green as "changes to be committed." Experiment.java stays red in the working directory, deliberately excluded. The staging area now holds exactly the intended change.

Step 3: The engineer runs git commit. Git takes the staged snapshot and records it in the local repository as a new commit with a hash, author, timestamp, and message. This happens entirely offline. The staging area is now clean, and the commit lives in the local dot-git history.

Step 4: A teammate has pushed a change to main. The engineer runs git fetch, which downloads those commits into the local repository and updates origin/main, but does not alter the working directory or current branch. The engineer inspects the incoming commits safely.

Step 5: The engineer runs git merge origin/main to integrate the teammate's work into the feature branch, resolving any conflict. Had they run git pull instead, Git would have done this fetch-plus-merge in one step.

Step 6: With the branch now up to date and ahead of the remote, the engineer runs git push. The local commit uploads to the remote branch, becoming visible to the whole team. The change has traveled the full pipeline: working directory, staging, local repository, remote.

```
Oct 25, 2026 03:40:02 AM INFO: working dir: 3 files modified (red)
Oct 25, 2026 03:40:10 AM INFO: git add: 2 files staged (green), Experiment.java excluded
Oct 25, 2026 03:40:20 AM INFO: git commit: snapshot TRF-77 saved to local repo (offline)
Oct 25, 2026 03:41:02 AM INFO: git fetch: downloaded 1 teammate commit to origin/main
Oct 25, 2026 03:41:30 AM INFO: git merge origin/main: integrated, 0 conflicts
Oct 25, 2026 03:41:45 AM INFO: git push: commit published to remote feature/transfer-limit
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ┌────────────────────┐   git add    ┌────────────────────┐
  │ WORKING DIRECTORY  │─────────────▶│ STAGING AREA        │
  │ edit files on disk │              │ (index): choose     │
  │ TransferLimit.java │◀─────────────│ exactly what commits│
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Locations, States, and Commands ═══

  ┌─ Four Locations + Commands ──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Working Dir  : files you edit (modified/untracked)          │
  │  Staging Area : index — what goes in the next commit         │
  │  Local Repo   : .git — committed snapshots (offline)         │
  │  Remote Repo  : shared server copy                           │
  │  add    : working dir -> staging                             │
  │  commit : staging -> local repo                              │
  │  push   : local repo -> remote                               │
  │  fetch  : remote -> local (refs only, no working-dir change) │
  │  pull   : remote -> local + merge into current branch        │
  │  restore: staging -> working dir (unstage) / discard edit    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── File State Diagram ─────────────────────────────────────

  [untracked/modified] ──git add──→ [staged] ──git commit──→ [committed local]
         ▲                   │                                     │ git push
         │ git restore       │ git restore --staged                ▼
         └───────────────────┘                             [committed remote]

  [committed remote] ──git fetch──→ [in local refs: origin/*]
                      ──git pull───→ [merged into working branch]

  ── Command Contracts ──────────────────────────────────────

  git add <file>   Pre: file modified   Post: change in staging
  git commit -m    Pre: something staged Post: new snapshot in local repo
  git push         Pre: local ahead, not behind  Post: remote updated
  git fetch        Pre: remote reachable Post: origin/* refs updated only
  git pull         = fetch + merge ; may create merge commit / conflict

  ── Call Chain (edit -> share) ─────────────────────────────

  1. edit files           (working directory)
  2. git add <2 files>    (-> staging, exclude Experiment.java)
  3. git commit -m ...    (-> local repo, offline)
  4. git fetch origin     (<- remote refs, inspect)
  5. git merge origin/main(integrate teammate work)
  6. git push             (-> remote, team sees it)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Git organizes code across four locations, and understanding them is the key to understanding Git. The working directory is the folder of files I actually edit on disk; a changed file here is modified but not yet tracked for a commit. The staging area, also called the index, is a holding area where I declare exactly which changes belong in the next commit — this is what lets me commit two related files while leaving an unrelated experiment out. The local repository is the dot-git database on my machine where commits are stored as permanent snapshots, entirely offline. The remote repository is the shared copy on a server like GitHub that the whole team uses as the common meeting point.

The commands form a clear forward pipeline. git add moves a change from the working directory into the staging area, so I pick precisely what goes into the commit. git commit takes everything staged and records it as a new snapshot in the local repository, with a hash, author, timestamp, and message, and it needs no network, which is why Git is distributed and I can commit offline. git push uploads my local commits to the remote so teammates can see them.

Bringing others' work down has two commands with an important difference. git fetch downloads new commits from the remote into my local repository and updates the remote-tracking references like origin/main, but it does not touch my working directory or current branch, so I can inspect incoming changes safely first. git pull is a convenience that does a fetch followed immediately by a merge into my current branch, downloading and applying in one step. I generally prefer fetch then merge in deliberate situations, because it lets me review before integrating, whereas pull can surprise me with an immediate merge or conflict.

At National Bank of India I use this model every day. When I added a transfer-limit feature, I edited several files, staged only the two that belonged to that logical change so the commit stayed focused and reviewable, committed locally, fetched a teammate's recent change to inspect it safely, merged it in, and finally pushed. The mental model I keep is a one-way forward flow — edit, add, commit, push — with fetch and pull flowing down to receive others' work, plus restore and reset to move changes backward when I need to undo.
